primaryPain: A status report for executives usually arrives as a project report with the headline buried somewhere in the middle, so a leader has to read three paragraphs of progress to find the one line that needs them.

painBullets: The committee spends its time being briefed on progress instead of resolving the items only it can resolve.

whyHardHeading: Why this gets hard at scale
whyHard: A standing committee meets on a cadence, but risk does not, so the template has to surface what changed since last time, not just where things stand today.
Across a portfolio, each program lead formats their update differently, and the committee cannot compare apples that were prepared as oranges.
Filling the template honestly takes hours of chasing owners, so it gets done fast and shallow exactly when the program is under strain.
howHusnHelps: Husn fills the template from Jira, Slack, and docs, so the agenda, RAG, decisions, and escalations arrive drafted rather than blank.
It grounds each RAG color in evidence and flags where the data disagrees with the rating, so green has to earn it.
It carries forward open decisions and aging escalations automatically, so nothing the committee owns quietly drops off the page.

title: Weekly executive project summary
metaDescription: A weekly summary for executives of what actually moved across projects. Husn reads Jira, Slack, and docs and writes the few changes worth a leader's attention.
heroHeadline: What moved this week, in one read.
heroSubheadline: Executives do not need a recap of everything that happened. They need the handful of things that changed. Husn writes that weekly summary from the work itself.
primaryPain: The weekly executive summary is usually a copy-paste of the team's standup notes, so a leader gets a week of activity to wade through and still cannot tell what is different from last Friday.
painBullets: Activity and change get blurred together, so steady progress reads the same as a project quietly going off the rails.
Each week's summary is written from scratch, so the thread between this week and last gets lost and trends never surface.
Whoever writes it includes what they remember, which means the inconvenient changes are the ones most likely to be left out.
whyHardHeading: Why this gets hard at scale
whyHard: Summarizing a week across a portfolio means holding dozens of moving parts in mind at once, which no one does reliably under a Friday deadline.
A weekly cadence only helps if the summary captures the delta, and computing the delta by hand across tools is exactly the slow part people skip.
The more projects there are, the more a thin summary hides, because the one that moved is averaged in with the nine that did not.
howHusnHelps: Husn reads across Jira, Slack, and docs each week and writes the summary automatically, leading with what changed since the last one.
It compares this week to last and surfaces drift, slipped dates, and new risks rather than restating steady progress.
Every change in the summary links back to its source, so a leader can see exactly what moved and where.

title: AI-generated project summaries
metaDescription: AI that summarizes projects from the work itself: Jira, Slack, and docs reconciled into an accurate, sourced summary. Husn never guesses and never writes back.
heroEyebrow: Summaries from the work, not the writer
heroHeadline: Project summaries drawn from the work.
heroSubheadline: A summary is only useful if it is accurate. Husn summarizes each project from Jira, Slack, and docs, reconciles what they say, and links every line back to its source.
primaryPain: Most AI summary tools paraphrase whatever text you paste in, so they confidently summarize one Slack thread or one ticket and miss the contradiction sitting in a document nobody fed them.
painBullets: A summary built from a single source inherits that source's blind spots and reads as authoritative anyway.
Generic summarizers smooth language fluently but cannot tell a resolved blocker from an open one, so the gist can be wrong.
Without a link back to evidence, a reader cannot tell which sentences are grounded and which the model filled in.
whyHardHeading: Why this gets hard at scale
whyHard: Accurate summarization means reconciling sources that disagree, which is hard to do by hand and impossible to do well across a whole portfolio.
The more a summary is trusted, the more a confident wrong sentence costs, so fluency without grounding becomes a liability as adoption grows.
Projects change daily, so a summary has to be regenerated from current state, not written once and quietly left to age.
howHusnHelps: Husn generates each summary from Jira, Slack, and docs together, reconciling what they say rather than paraphrasing one source.
It writes only what the evidence supports and leads with what changed and what carries risk, so the summary is grounded, not guessed.
Every sentence links back to the issue, message, or document behind it, so a reader can check any claim in a click.

painBullets: Each layer between the work and leadership softens the bad news, so the version at the top is the least accurate one in the chain.

Writing an honest report under pressure is slow and uncomfortable, so it gets shortened and softened when the stakes are highest.
